read: full: all 7 pages (abstract, introduction, related work, section 3 composition, construction pipeline and evaluation protocol, section 4 experiments, conclusion, references)
venue_now: arXiv preprint only: arXiv:2507.04766v1, 7 Jul 2025 (p.1); the file is the whole 7-page v1. cited_set_resolution.md: arXiv only as of 2026-10.
what_it_is: A physics benchmark of 500 problems that each require one numerical answer, in two parts: Phy_A, 400 static graduate- or olympiad-level problems, and Phy_B, 100 problems whose numerical constants are perturbed by a variation engine to produce variants with the same physical model (pp.1-3). Problems were collected from textbooks and exam papers, OCR'd, manually annotated, rewritten in context by DeepSeek-R1 with manual review, verified by one to two annotators who solved them step by step, and paraphrased by an independent reviewer (p.3). Answers count as correct within 1% relative error, and a Phy_B problem is credited only if every variant is solved (p.2, p.4). The best model solves 43.0% of Phy_A; accuracy falls by 22.5% on average from the original Phy_B problems to their variants (p.2, p.4).
domain: advanced undergraduate, graduate and olympiad physics: classical mechanics, electromagnetism, optics, quantum physics, electrodynamics, semiconductor and fluid mechanics, atomic physics (p.3)
size: 500 problems (Phy_A 400 static; Phy_B 100 parameterised, released with three variants each); 15 models in Table 2 (p.3, p.4)
source_of_items: textbooks and exam papers, rewritten by DeepSeek-R1 with manual review and paraphrased by an independent reviewer; Phy_B variants generated by perturbing numerical constants (p.3)
instances: static (Phy_A) and generated by numerical perturbation (Phy_B) (p.3, Table 1)
has_gold_traces: partial: ground-truth LaTeX solutions exist and drive the Phy_B variation engine (p.3), and annotators solved each problem step by step (p.3), but the solutions are not described as released and play no part in scoring
evaluation: final answer: a LaTeX-based parser converts the output to a number, accepted if the relative error is at most 1%; units and significant figures are specified in each question; Phy_B requires all variants correct (p.2, p.4)
human_validation: Manual extraction and annotation; DeepSeek-R1 rewrites manually reviewed; every question and solution independently verified by one to two annotators who solved it step by step; symbolic derivations and numerical end points independently produced and cross-verified (p.3). No counts of corrected or dropped items and no agreement statistics are reported.
contamination_measures: generated variants (Phy_B numerical perturbation, p.3); every question paraphrased by an independent reviewer to reduce overlap with pre-training corpora (p.3); scenario rewrites by DeepSeek-R1 (p.3)

engtrace_use.sentence: S-P1 (L172-177): '... others target advanced symbolic (Zhang et al., 2025b; Qiu et al., 2025) or qualitative (Wang et al., 2023; Shojaee et al., 2025) understanding.' S-P2 (L177-180, uncited, covers all six): 'Despite this progress, these benchmarks remain confined to theoretical physics, lacking the integrative context of engineering.' Rebuttal R-1 (July 2026): 'ABench-Physics (Zhang et al., 2025b) uses a 1% tolerance for physics reasoning.'
engtrace_use.explanation: 'Advanced' fits (graduate and olympiad level, p.1, p.3), but 'symbolic' contradicts the paper: ABench-Physics 'focuses exclusively on numerical calculation problems' and defines itself against benchmarks that 'required answers in the form of expressions (Qiu et al., 2025b), which are difficult to evaluate precisely' (p.2; also p.1, p.5), that is, against PHYBench, the paper the May sentence pairs it with. The May text also omits the feature most relevant to EngTrace, the dynamic Phy_B subset generated by perturbing numerical constants to resist memorisation (pp.1-3), which bears on EngTrace's claim to generated, contamination-resistant instances. S-P2's 'theoretical physics' is loose (the syllabus includes semiconductor and fluid mechanics, p.3). The rebuttal use R-1 is accurate: answers are accepted within 1% relative error (p.2, p.4). If 'symbolic' were read loosely as 'requiring symbolic derivation', the verdict would be misleading rather than wrong; I do not think that reading is natural next to 'qualitative'.

suggested_wording: ABench-Physics (Zhang et al., 2025b) pairs 400 static graduate- and olympiad-level problems with 100 whose numerical constants are perturbed to produce variants, crediting a model only when it solves every variant, and accepts numerical answers within 1% relative error.
facts_to_cite: 500 problems with single numerical answers: Phy_A, 400 static graduate- or olympiad-level problems; Phy_B, 100 problems with a variation engine that perturbs the numerical constants in the ground-truth LaTeX solutions (p.1, p.3)
Numerical answers only, chosen explicitly over multiple-choice or expression answers (p.2)
Answers accepted within 1% relative error; each question specifies the unit and the number of significant figures (p.2, p.4)

A Phy_B problem is credited only if all its variants are answered correctly (p.2, p.4); the preprint releases three variants per Phy_B problem and the engine is still under development (p.3, footnote 2)
Best Phy_A accuracy 43.0% (Gemini 2.5 Pro with reasoning); average accuracy drop of 22.5% from the original to the perturbed Phy_B problems (p.2, p.4)
Every question was paraphrased by an independent reviewer to reduce overlap with pre-training corpora (p.3)
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: generated instances in the Phy_B subset, made by perturbing the numerical constants of a fixed solution, the same mechanism as a parameterised template (p.3); numerical answers checked against a relative tolerance (1%, against EngTrace's 0.2% or one unit in the last digit); a contamination argument built on variants. Lacks: generation at scale (100 parameterised problems, three variants each, p.3); gold traces used in evaluation; any step-level or process evaluation (final number only, p.4); an engineering domain; any validation of the evaluator or agreement statistics. Its all-variants-correct criterion differs from EngTrace's scoring of each instance separately.
notes: The facts are certain; the medium confidence concerns only the wrong/misleading boundary on 'symbolic'. Caveat for the rewrite: the 22.5% Phy_B drop compares single-problem accuracy with an all-three-variants-correct criterion (p.4), so part of it is mechanical and should not be repeated as evidence of memorisation without qualification, though the paper presents it that way (p.2). By my count, Table 2's delta column averages 0.225 over the 15 models listed, while the text says it evaluated 'four widely used large language models' (p.4), an internal inconsistency in the paper. Short 7-page arXiv-only preprint. Reference-list error (confirmed on p.1): all 12 printed first names are wrong (printed 'Yifan Zhang ... Jun Zhao'); the authors are Yiming Zhang, Yingfan Ma, Yanmei Gu, Zhengkai Yang, Yihong Zhuang, Feng Wang, Zenan Huang, Yuanyuan Wang, Chao Huang, Bowen Song, Cheng Lin, Junbo Zhao. Its 'Xie et al., 2025' is Chulin Xie's paper on memorisation in logical reasoning, not FinChain.
